newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Foreign ministers to talk about enlargement, Turkey.
newsitem.headline: Foreign ministers to talk about enlargement, Turkey.

text.p: European Union foreign ministers will examine the question of enlarging the bloc this weekend and touch on the controversial issue of the link with NATO's expansion plans.

Meeting for what is supposed to be a relaxed chat in the Dutch countryside, the ministers will also seek to present a coherent political line to Turkey following a sharp snub to Ankara last week from the bloc's centrist leaders.
The ministers are to meet on Saturday and Sunday in Apeldoorn, in the central Netherlands, for a twice-yearly informal gathering.

It is supposed to be an opportunity to discuss policy without the necessity of taking decisions. But Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo has set an agenda focusing on some of the most sensitive diplomatic issues facing the bloc.

One of these is the question over how to proceed in EU membership negotiations with 10 former communist bloc countries -- Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovenia, Slovakia, Bulgaria, Romania, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

All have been promised eventual membership, but the EU recognises that not all are even close to being ready to join. Nor has the bloc ever formally committed itself to beginning talks at the same time, saying only that it hopes negotiations will begin early next year.
As the date approaches, diplomats say, the EU is in two minds. One camp says talks should only begin with those clearly ready, such as Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
"To formally begin with a wide group of people, some of whom you know (are not going to make it) is bad politics," one EU official said.

The other camp favours talks beginning with all countries at once in a clear attempt not to show favouritism that would isolate countries still adjusting to true independence from the old Soviet Union.
After starting talks with everyone, it is argued, countries that did not pass muster could be let down gently.

The danger of leaving some countries out in the cold has also triggered behind-the-scenes lobbying by the United States for the Europeans to extend EU membership to some countries that will miss out on NATO enlargement.
"The Americans are pushing very hard for a clear link to be established," one EU diplomat said, adding that Estonia was the main target of the discussions.
Estonia, which is developing rapidly on the economic front, has been all but formally ruled out of being in the first wave of NATO enlargement because of its history and proximity to Russia.
Washington is said to be arguing that including it in the EU's first wave would show other countries, notably the Baltics, that they were not being deserted.

European officials have striven to dismiss any expansion link between the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation and the EU -- a stance likely to be repeated at the weekend when the relationship is discussed.

"I think the major message will be that there is not a link and that we don't want to be pressured by geo-strategic considerations from the central question: Is this country ready to join the European Union," the diplomat said.

As well as eastern Europe, the ministers will discuss the bloc's relations with Turkey -- thrown into a spin last week when German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and other centrist EU leaders said Ankara should not be allowed in to the EU.
Turkey has asked to join, but had its application rebuffed over a variety of issues, including human rights.
Diplomats said the EU ministers would try to formulate a policy for the whole bloc on the matter.
